text_blocks.snippet: Several CAR T-cell therapies are FDA-approved to treat certain types of blood cancers, including specific leukemias and lymphomas. These therapies involve genetically modifying a patient's own T cells to target and destroy cancer cells.
snippet_highlighted_words: to treat certain types of blood cancers, including specific leukemias and lymphomas

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of the key aspects:

list.snippet: CAR T-cell therapy is a type of immunotherapy where a patient's T cells are collected and genetically modified in a lab to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR).
The CAR is designed to recognize and bind to a specific protein (antigen) on cancer cells.
These engineered T cells, now called CAR T cells, are then multiplied in the lab and infused back into the patient to attack and destroy the cancer cells.

Tisagenlecleucel (Kymriah): Approved for relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in patients up to 25 years old, and for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma in adults.
Axicabtagene ciloleucel (Yescarta): Approved for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma and follicular lymphoma in adults.
Brexucabtagene autoleucel (Tecartus): Approved for relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma in adults.
Idecabtagene vicleucel (Abecma): Approved for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma in adults who have received at least four prior lines of therapy.
Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (Carvykti): Approved for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma in adults who have received at least four prior lines of therapy.
Lisocabtagene maraleucel (Breyanzi): Approved for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma and mantle cell lymphoma in adults.
Obecabtagene autoleucel (Autocatzyl): Approved for adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL.
CAR T-cell therapy is a complex and potentially risky treatment.
It is associated with side effects, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity (ICANS).
Careful patient selection and management by experienced medical teams are crucial.
Clinical trials are ongoing to explore the use of CAR T-cell therapy for other cancers and to improve its efficacy and safety.
